scenes.narration: Welcome back. With KCL and KVL we can now solve circuits. But some circuits are much easier to solve if we first reshape them. Remember Part 4, where we saw that a real voltage source has a resistance in series, and a real current source has a resistance in parallel? Today we discover that these two are secretly interchangeable. This trick is called source transformation, and it can turn a messy circuit into a simple one in a few steps.
scenes.title: SOURCE TRANSFORMATION
scenes.subtitle: Swap a voltage source for a current source, and back

scenes.narration: On the left, a twelve volt source with a four ohm resistor in series. On the right, a three ampere current source with the same four ohm resistor in parallel. Now we connect the same load to both. Watch the meters. With an eight ohm load, both give one ampere and eight volts. Now the load changes to two ohms: both give two amperes and four volts. And with twenty ohms: both give half an ampere and ten volts. Whatever load we connect, the two circuits behave exactly the same. From the outside, you cannot tell them apart.

Here is the rule. A voltage source V s in series with a resistor R can be replaced by a current source I s in parallel with the same resistor R, where I s equals V s divided by R. And it works the other way too: a current source I s in parallel with R becomes a voltage source V s equals I s times R, in series with R. The resistor value never changes. Only its position changes, from series to parallel.
scenes.formula: I_s = V_s / R          V_s = I_s × R

scenes.narration: Why are they the same? Look at the terminals. With nothing connected, the voltage source circuit gives its full twelve volts, because no current flows through R. The current source circuit pushes all three amperes through the four ohm resistor, which also gives twelve volts. Now short the terminals together. The voltage source pushes twelve over four, three amperes. The current source sends all three amperes through the short. Same open circuit voltage, same short circuit current, so the same straight line for every load in between.
example: Same two end points → same line → same behaviour

scenes.narration: One detail you must never get wrong is the direction. The arrow of the current source must point towards the terminal that was the positive terminal of the voltage source. Think about it: the voltage source pushes current out of its plus terminal, so the current source must push current out at that same point. If you flip the arrow, every answer will come out with the wrong sign.
scenes.title: Keep the polarity

parts.label: Current arrow points to that same terminal
Current leaves at + in both circuits

scenes.narration: Source transformation has two limits. First, it only works for practical sources. An ideal voltage source has no series resistor, so dividing by zero gives an infinite current: impossible. An ideal current source has no parallel resistor, so there is nothing to convert. Second, the two circuits are equivalent only at the terminals. Inside, they can behave differently. For example, with no load connected, the current source circuit still burns power in its resistor, while the voltage source circuit burns none. So use the swap to find load voltages and currents, not internal power.
scenes.title: Two limits

parts.label: Use it for load values, not internal power

scenes.narration: Here is how engineers use it. Suppose two practical voltage sources are connected in parallel to a load. Adding them directly is messy. So follow these steps. One: convert each voltage source into a current source with its resistor in parallel. Two: now the current sources are all in parallel, so simply add them. Three: combine the parallel resistors into one. Four: if you want, convert back into a single voltage source with one series resistor. Now the whole circuit is one source and one resistor feeding the load.
scenes.title: Simplify with source transformation
items: Convert each V-source + series R → I-source + parallel R
Convert back to one V-source + series R (optional)

scenes.narration: Let's do it. Source one: twelve volts with four ohms. Source two: six volts with two ohms. Both are connected in parallel to a load. Convert: twelve over four gives three amperes with four ohms, and six over two gives three amperes with two ohms. Add the currents: six amperes. Combine the resistors: four in parallel with two is eight over six, about one point three three ohms. Convert back: six amperes times one point three three ohms is eight volts. So the two sources act like one eight volt source with one point three three ohms in series. With a two point six seven ohm load, the current is eight divided by four, two amperes.
scenes.formula: 12 V,4 Ω ∥ 6 V,2 Ω  →  8 V with 1.33 Ω

scenes.narration: Let's check that final result is truly equivalent. On the left is our eight volt source with one point three three ohms in series. On the right, its current source form: six amperes with one point three three ohms in parallel. Watch both meters as the load changes. They always agree. This is how we can trust a simplified circuit: it gives exactly the same answers at the terminals.

Source transformation is a tool you will use again and again. It simplifies circuits before mesh or nodal analysis, so you need fewer equations. It is the bridge between Thevenin's theorem and Norton's theorem, which we will meet soon: a Thevenin circuit is a voltage source with series R, a Norton circuit is a current source with parallel R, and source transformation converts one into the other. And it is used to model transistors and amplifiers in whichever form is easier.
scenes.title: Where it is used

scenes.narration: Let's bring it together. A voltage source with a series resistor is equivalent to a current source with the same resistor in parallel. I s equals V s over R, and V s equals I s times R. The current arrow points towards the old positive terminal. It works only for practical sources, and only at the terminals. And it lets us combine sources and simplify circuits before solving them.
scenes.title: Source transformation in one picture

parts.label: V_s + series R ⇄ I_s + parallel R

scenes.narration: Source transformation helped when resistors were in series or in parallel. But some networks have resistors connected in a triangle or a Y shape, which are neither series nor parallel. In the next part, we learn the star-delta transformation, which turns these tricky shapes into simple ones.
scenes.title: NEXT: STAR-DELTA TRANSFORMATION
